prompt: A checker reports `Unsupported operand types for * ("float" and "None")` on a line that has run a thousand times in production. What did it read to know that?
hint: It followed something to its `return`.

choices.text: A log of the thousand runs, where a `None` appeared once
choices.why: It read no log and no data at all — that is what static means.

choices.text: The annotations, and the `return` of the function whose result lands there
choices.why: It followed `find` to its `return`, saw `dict.get` answers `None` for a missing key, and looked at line 7.

choices.text: The database it connects to, to see which currency codes are present in the rates table
choices.why: It opened no file and made no connection.

choices.text: The test suite, which covers the line with one case that fails
choices.why: It ran no test. The line has no failing case, which is precisely why nobody had found this.

prompt: Which of these does a checker find in a file with no annotations in it at all?
hint: Two of the errors in this lesson need no types.

choices.text: A multiplication by something that turned out to be `None`
choices.why: That needs the annotation saying the value is `float | None`.

choices.text: A call with more arguments than the function takes
choices.why: Arity is structural: `Too many arguments` is reported whatever the types are.

choices.text: A function returning a string on one branch and an integer on another
choices.why: A return type has to be declared before a return value disagrees with it.

choices.text: A `dict` whose values are strings where integers were expected
choices.why: With nothing annotated there is no expectation to compare against.

prompt: `def average(values: list[float]) -> float: return sum(values) * len(values)`. What does a checker say?
hint: Every type in it lines up.

choices.text: It warns that `*` appears where `/` was meant, and names the line it is written on
choices.why: That would require knowing what an average is, which is outside what a type says.

choices.text: Nothing — the types are right and the arithmetic is not its subject
choices.why: `sum` of floats times an integer is a float, so the annotation holds. The formula is wrong and no checker has an opinion about that.

choices.text: `Unsupported operand types for * ("float" and "int")`, reported on the return line
choices.why: Multiplying a float by an integer is ordinary arithmetic and the checker knows it.

choices.text: `Incompatible return value type (got "int", expected "float")`
choices.why: A float times an integer is a float, so the return type is satisfied.

prompt: `row = {"city": "Recife"}` then `row["citty"]`. `mypy` answers `Success: no issues found`. Why?
hint: What is the declared type of `row`?

choices.text: String keys are compared after normalisation, so the two spellings match
choices.why: No normalisation happens anywhere, and the two spellings are different keys.

choices.text: The dictionary literal is too short for the checker to infer a key type from it at all
choices.why: It inferred `dict[str, str]` from the literal without difficulty.

choices.text: Subscripting is outside what a static checker looks at
choices.why: Subscripting is checked — on a `TypedDict` the same line is reported by name.

choices.text: A `dict[str, str]` accepts any string as a key, so the typo is a valid expression
choices.why: The type says the keys are strings, and `"citty"` is a string. It raises `KeyError` at run time.

prompt: The same lookup, with `Row` declared as a `TypedDict`. What is reported?
hint: It gets a suggestion underneath.

choices.text: `TypedDict "Row" has no key "citty"`, with a `Did you mean "city"?` note
choices.why: A `TypedDict` names its keys, so the checker has something to compare the spelling against.

choices.text: A warning rather than an error, since the key might be added later
choices.why: It is an error with the code `typeddict-item`.

choices.text: `"Row" has no attribute "citty"`, because a `TypedDict` is a class
choices.why: Attribute access and key access are different errors; this one is `typeddict-item`.

choices.text: The same `Success` — a `TypedDict` is a `dict` at run time
choices.why: It is a `dict` at run time, and the annotation exists for the checker, which reads it.

prompt: `app/report.py:4: error: Argument 1 to "find" has incompatible type "int"; expected "str"  [arg-type]`. Which part do you put inside a `# type: ignore[...]`?
hint: The part in brackets at the end.

choices.text: `arg-type`
choices.why: The bracketed error code is what `# type: ignore[...]`, `disable_error_code` and a search engine all take.

choices.text: `Argument 1 to "find"`, which identifies what is being ignored
choices.why: The sentence is for the reader; the bracketed code is what the tool parses.

choices.text: `incompatible type`, which is the category of the failure
choices.why: That is prose inside the sentence, not an error code.

choices.text: `report.py:4`, which identifies the line being silenced
choices.why: The comment goes on the line, so the location is already known.

prompt: `Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 3 source files)`. What are the other two files?
hint: Something had to be read to understand the one you asked about.

choices.text: Files in the cache from the previous run, re-checked to confirm they are unchanged
choices.why: The cache avoids work; it does not add files to the count.

choices.text: The two stub files that shipped with the standard library modules in use
choices.why: Standard-library stubs are read and are not counted as source files here.

choices.text: Files with errors that were suppressed by an ignore comment somewhere
choices.why: A suppressed error would not raise the checked count.

choices.text: Modules it imported, read so the checker knows what the names mean
choices.why: Errors are reported in what you asked about; imports are read to understand it.

prompt: You run `mypy app/rates.py` and get `Success: no issues found in 1 source file`. The project has a real type error. Where is it?
hint: Who calls `rates`?

choices.text: In a stub file, which is reported separately from source
choices.why: Stub errors would still appear in the output.

choices.text: Nowhere yet — the error appears after the cache is cleared
choices.why: The cache changes speed, not verdicts.

choices.text: In a file that calls something in `rates.py` with the wrong type
choices.why: `rates.py` is internally consistent. The disagreement is at the call site, in a file you did not ask about.

choices.text: Inside `rates.py`, in a function body the checker skipped
choices.why: That is possible in principle, and here the error is in `report.py`, which the run did not cover.

prompt: What does `reveal_type(data)` require you to import for the checker to answer?
hint: The checker recognises the bare name.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: The checker treats the bare name specially and replies with a `note`. At run time the bare name raises `NameError`.

choices.text: `from typing import reveal_type`, which is what defines it
choices.why: That import gives you a real function for run time; the checker needs no import.

choices.text: `import typing`, and then the qualified name
choices.why: The qualified form works at run time and is not what the checker requires.

choices.text: `from mypy import reveal_type`, which is shipped with the checker
choices.why: No such import exists.

prompt: The directory `mypy` writes its incremental results into, which belongs in `.gitignore`: `______/`
hint: It is named after the tool.

prompt: `def add(a, b): return a + b` and then `add("x", 3)`. Default settings. What is reported?
hint: What does the checker know about `a`?

choices.text: Nothing — an unannotated function is one the checker has no opinion about
choices.why: With no annotation there is no expectation to violate, so the call is unjudged.

choices.text: `Unsupported operand types for + ("str" and "int")`
choices.why: That would need the parameters annotated.

choices.text: A note that the arguments are of differing types
choices.why: The checker has no declared types here to compare.

choices.text: `Function is missing a type annotation`, since the call forced the issue
choices.why: That is `no-untyped-def`, which arrives with `disallow_untyped_defs`.

prompt: Same unannotated `add`, but the call is `add(1, 2, 3)`. Default settings.
hint: One thing is structural.

choices.text: Nothing, for the same reason the previous call was unjudged
choices.why: Types were unjudged; the number of arguments is a separate and structural question.

choices.text: `Argument 3 has incompatible type "int"`, naming the extra one
choices.why: There is no third parameter for it to have a type against.

choices.text: `Too many arguments for "add"`
choices.why: Arity is checked whatever the types are: three arguments into two parameters is wrong on its face.

choices.text: A note suggesting `*args`, which is what would accept three
choices.why: The checker suggests no rewrite here.

prompt: Which `--strict` flag stops a typed function from resting on an unannotated one?
hint: It is about calls, not definitions.

choices.text: `disallow_untyped_calls`
choices.why: It reports `Call to untyped function "…" in typed context`, which is what keeps the checked half from quietly leaning on the unchecked half.

choices.text: `disallow_untyped_defs`, which requires every function to be annotated
choices.why: That is about the definition. The call is a separate flag and a separate error code.

choices.text: `disallow_any_generics`, which rejects a bare `dict` or `list`
choices.why: That is about missing type parameters on a generic.

choices.text: `warn_return_any`, which rejects handing back something untyped
choices.why: That is about what a function returns, not about what it calls.

prompt: `def load(path: str) -> dict: return json.load(f)`. Which two errors does `--strict` add?
hint: One is the bare `dict`, one is what `json.load` gives back.

choices.text: `type-arg` on the bare `dict`, and `no-any-return`
choices.why: `disallow_any_generics` wants `dict[str, int]`, and `warn_return_any` refuses to let `Any` become the declared return silently.

choices.text: `Missing type parameters` and `Call to untyped function "load"`
choices.why: `load` is annotated, so `no-untyped-call` does not apply to it.

choices.text: `Function is missing a type annotation` and `Returning Any`
choices.why: The function is annotated, so `no-untyped-def` does not fire.

choices.text: `Incompatible return value type (got "Any", expected "dict")`
choices.why: The error code for this is `no-any-return` and its wording is `Returning Any from function declared to return`.

prompt: What makes `check_untyped_defs` the cheapest flag to turn on across an existing codebase?
hint: Think about what it asks somebody to write.

choices.text: It silences whatever errors are inside unannotated functions until somebody annotates them
choices.why: It does the opposite: by default those bodies are skipped, and this turns them on.

choices.text: It infers annotations for the unannotated functions and writes them back into the file
choices.why: It writes nothing. Inference for a report is not a rewrite of your source.

choices.text: It checks inside bodies that already exist and asks nobody to write an annotation
choices.why: The signatures stay as they are, and the errors it finds are defects rather than paperwork.

choices.text: It limits the run to the modules that already carry annotations throughout their bodies
choices.why: It widens what is checked rather than narrowing it.

prompt: Why do the settings belong in `pyproject.toml` rather than in the command you type?
hint: Three places run the checker.

choices.text: Because a flag on the command line is ignored when a config file exists
choices.why: A command-line flag takes precedence over the file, which is part of the problem.

choices.text: So your editor, your terminal and CI run the same check
choices.why: A flag passed on one machine and not in CI is a green build in one place and a red one in the other, for the same commit.

choices.text: Because the command line has no equivalent for most of the settings
choices.why: Almost every setting has a matching flag; the point is agreement between the places that run it.

choices.text: Because the cache is keyed by the file and is discarded when a flag differs
choices.why: Cache invalidation is a consequence here, not the reason to keep settings in a file.

prompt: What does `python_version = "3.12"` decide?
hint: It is about what the checker believes exists.

choices.text: Which interpreter the checker launches in order to import and inspect your modules
choices.why: It launches no interpreter and imports nothing — it reads files.

choices.text: Which `py.typed` marker files among your installed dependencies are honoured
choices.why: The marker is honoured or not on its own, regardless of the target version.

choices.text: Which version of `mypy` is installed by `pip install mypy`
choices.why: The checker's own version is chosen by whatever pins it, not by this setting.

choices.text: Which syntax and which standard-library signatures the checker believes in
choices.why: Set it to what you deploy on, or the checker judges your code against a different language than the one that will run it.

prompt: The double-bracket table in `pyproject.toml` that loosens a flag for named modules: `[[tool.mypy.______]]`
hint: TOML calls this shape an array of tables.

prompt: Strict at the top, `disallow_untyped_defs = false` in an override naming `app.legacy.*`. What happens to `app/legacy/old.py`?
hint: The override turns one flag off for one place.

choices.text: It is still checked, and the missing annotation is no longer an error there
choices.why: Every other flag still applies to it, and the rest of the package stays strict.

choices.text: It is skipped, so nothing inside it is reported
choices.why: Skipping is what `exclude` does. An override changes a flag and keeps the module checked.

choices.text: It is checked and its errors are downgraded to `note` lines
choices.why: There is no downgrade mechanism; the flag is off and that error is not produced.

choices.text: It is checked only when something else imports it
choices.why: It is in `files`, so it is checked in its own right.

prompt: Why is `exclude` the wrong tool for a directory you are not ready to check?
hint: An excluded module still has a relationship with the rest.

choices.text: `exclude` takes a regular expression, which is easy to write wrongly
choices.why: It does take one, and a correct expression still leaves you with the import problem.

choices.text: An excluded module is still imported by the ones you check
choices.why: You end up with a report that is confusing rather than smaller. An override with loosened flags keeps it checked at a level it passes.

choices.text: `exclude` and `files` contradict each other and the checker refuses to start
choices.why: They combine without complaint.

choices.text: `exclude` is applied after the cache is written, so the run is no faster
choices.why: Speed is not the objection here.

prompt: `def total(items):` with a bad assignment in its body. `mypy` emits a note; `pyright` reports an error. Why?
hint: One of them skips something by default.

choices.text: `mypy` treats an unannotated parameter as `Any`, which absorbs the error
choices.why: `Any` in the parameter does not explain it: the assignment has a declared type of its own.

choices.text: `mypy` skips the bodies of unannotated functions by default and `pyright` checks them
choices.why: `check_untyped_defs` is the flag that makes the two agree on this file.

choices.text: `pyright` infers annotations for the parameters, which `mypy` declines to do
choices.why: Both infer within a body; the difference is that one of them declines to look at this body at all.

choices.text: `pyright` is running in strict mode and `mypy` in its default
choices.why: The `pyright` run here is in its default `standard` mode.

prompt: The same assignment. `mypy` says `variable has type "int"`; `pyright` says `Type "Literal['no']"`. What is the difference?
hint: One is telling you more about the value.

choices.text: `pyright` narrows to the exact value in its message where `mypy` names the wider type
choices.why: Both verdicts are the same; one report carries more information about what was on the right-hand side.

choices.text: `Literal['no']` is the declared type and `int` is the one that was inferred
choices.why: It is the other way round: the narrower name describes the expression on the right.

choices.text: `mypy` has not read the assignment yet and is reporting the declaration alone
choices.why: It read the assignment — that is what it is reporting.

choices.text: `pyright` is reporting a different error, on a different line of the same file, at the same time
choices.why: Same line, same file, same error.

prompt: Which values may `typeCheckingMode` take, and which is the default?
hint: There are four, and the default is not the loosest or the strictest.

choices.text: `off`, `basic`, `standard` and `strict`, with `standard` as the default
choices.why: Each rule underneath also has a name of its own and can be set to `error`, `warning` or `none`.

choices.text: `off`, `basic` and `strict`, with `basic` as the default
choices.why: `standard` sits between `basic` and `strict` and is the default.

choices.text: `none`, `warning` and `error`, with `warning` as the default
choices.why: Those three are the settings for an individual rule, not for the mode.

choices.text: `lenient`, `standard` and `pedantic`, with `standard` as the default
choices.why: Those names belong to no checker here.

prompt: A file carries `# pyright: ignore[reportAssignmentType]` on a line both checkers dislike. What does `mypy` do?
hint: One of them does not know that syntax.

choices.text: It reports the error, because that comment means nothing to it
choices.why: If a project runs both, the portable comment is `# type: ignore[code]`, which both honour.

choices.text: It honours the comment, since both read the same suppression syntax
choices.why: `mypy` reads `# type: ignore`; the `pyright:` form is not its syntax.

choices.text: It reports the comment itself as an unrecognised directive
choices.why: It treats the line as an ordinary comment and says nothing about it.

choices.text: It downgrades the error to a note, having seen that somebody decided
choices.why: There is no such downgrade.

prompt: What makes `pyright` the one in the editor?
hint: Something is already running as you type.

choices.text: It writes no cache directory of its own, so it leaves the working tree clean for you
choices.why: A cache directory in `.gitignore` is not what decides which checker an editor runs.

choices.text: It is the checker with a language-server protocol implementation of its own, shipped ready
choices.why: A language server exists for the other one too; speed and default packaging decided this.

choices.text: It is what Pylance runs, and it answers fast enough to report while you type
choices.why: It also reports `line:column`, so an error lands on the right half of a long line.

choices.text: It reads the `pyproject.toml` that editors already parse for other tooling
choices.why: Both read `pyproject.toml`, so that settles nothing between them.

prompt: `error: Library stubs not installed for "yaml"  [import-untyped]`. What is the first thing to try?
hint: The next line of the output tells you.

choices.text: Annotate the values coming out of the library as `Any` at each call
choices.why: That throws away the checking at exactly the boundary where it was available.

choices.text: Add `ignore_missing_imports = true` at the top of the config
choices.why: That silences the message for everything, including an import you misspelled.

choices.text: Add `# type: ignore[import-untyped]` to the import line
choices.why: It works and it buys a silence where a stub package would have bought types.

choices.text: Install the `types-PyYAML` package that the hint underneath names
choices.why: Hundreds of libraries have a `types-…` package written by other people, and it gives you real types rather than a silence.

prompt: What is the difference between `[import-untyped]` and `[import-not-found]`?
hint: One of the two libraries is installed.

choices.text: The first means it is installed with no types; the second means the module was not found
choices.why: The second is usually a typo, a missing install, or a `PYTHONPATH` the checker does not share.

choices.text: The first is a warning and the second is an error
choices.why: Both are errors.

choices.text: The first names a stub package that exists and the second names a source package that does not
choices.why: Both name a module; the difference is whether the checker found it at all.

choices.text: The first appears under `--strict` and the second in the default settings
choices.why: Both appear in the default settings.

prompt: The empty marker file a library puts in its package directory so its own annotations are honoured: `______`
hint: Two words joined by a dot.

prompt: `n: int = "a"  # type: ignore[arg-type]` where the real error code is `assignment`. What is reported?
hint: The narrow comment did not match.

choices.text: The error, plus a note saying the code is not covered by the comment
choices.why: A narrow ignore that stops matching starts reporting again, and the note names the mismatch.

choices.text: Nothing — a comment with any code in it silences the line
choices.why: A bare `# type: ignore` silences the line; one with a code silences that code.

choices.text: An error about the comment naming a code that does not apply
choices.why: The complaint is the original error; the mismatch arrives as a note beneath it.

choices.text: The error, downgraded to a warning because somebody had decided about the line
choices.why: It stays an error.

prompt: What does `warn_unused_ignores` report, and why does it earn its place before the rest of `--strict`?
hint: Think about a comment whose reason has gone.

choices.text: A `# type: ignore` on a line that a later edit moved
choices.why: The comment moves with the line it is on.

choices.text: `Unused "type: ignore" comment` — a suppression that silences nothing and misrepresents the file
choices.why: The stub was fixed or the code changed, and the comment stayed behind lying about the state of the file.

choices.text: A `# type: ignore` written without a bracketed error code
choices.why: That is a separate concern and this flag says nothing about it.

choices.text: A `# type: ignore` whose code is spelled wrongly
choices.why: That produces the `not covered by` note on the original error instead.

prompt: Twenty thousand lines, no annotations. What goes into CI on day one?
hint: Think about what has to exist before a bar can be raised.

choices.text: The checker with almost nothing turned on, reporting almost nothing
choices.why: The pipeline now has a step that can go red, and every later step raises the bar on something that already runs.

choices.text: `--strict`, so the size of the problem is visible from the start
choices.why: Four thousand errors is a number nobody acts on, and the usual next step is an ignore at the top of each file.

choices.text: The checker over one module, with the rest excluded from the run
choices.why: An excluded module is still imported by the ones you check, so its errors come back anyway.

choices.text: Nothing yet — annotate a first module, then add the step
choices.why: That leaves the step to be added on an afternoon when somebody remembers.

prompt: Which flag is the important one for stopping the untyped half from growing?
hint: It is about new code more than old code.

choices.text: `check_untyped_defs`, which starts checking inside the function bodies that already exist
choices.why: It is the cheapest first win and it says nothing about whether new code is annotated.

choices.text: `disallow_untyped_defs`, on by default with the unready modules listed as exceptions
choices.why: Every new module is then checked properly from its first line, and the list of exceptions can only shrink.

choices.text: `ignore_missing_imports`, which quiets the noise coming out of the third-party libraries first
choices.why: It removes noise from the report and has no bearing on your own new code.

choices.text: `warn_return_any`, which stops `Any` escaping through a return
choices.why: A good flag, and it does not decide whether a new function is annotated.

prompt: Why is "loose by default, strict on a list of ready modules" the wrong way round?
hint: Which arrangement changes colour when somebody adds an unannotated module?

choices.text: The checker reads the overrides before the top-level settings
choices.why: Order of precedence is defined and is not the objection here.

choices.text: Per-module strictness is not expressible in the override table
choices.why: It is expressible either way round; that is what makes the choice a real one.

choices.text: The list of ready modules grows faster than anybody maintains it
choices.why: A growing list of ready modules is progress; the problem is what happens outside it.

choices.text: The untyped half grows every week and nothing changes colour when it does
choices.why: Written the other way, a new unannotated module fails the build on the day it is written.

prompt: You are annotating a module. What comes first?
hint: One of the two is mostly worked out for you.

choices.text: The signatures — parameters and return types
choices.why: With those in place the locals are mostly inferred, so annotating them adds little.

choices.text: The locals, so the checker has something concrete to start from
choices.why: Locals are inferred from what is assigned to them; the signature is what the checker has no way to guess.

choices.text: The `# type: ignore` comments, so the run is quiet while you work
choices.why: That hides the work you are about to do from the tool doing it with you.

choices.text: The imports, rewritten to pull types from `typing` rather than built-ins
choices.why: Built-in generics are the current spelling and need no rewrite.

prompt: What is the one rule for the whole adoption process?
hint: It is about what a merge is allowed to add.

choices.text: No new suppression without a reason written beside it
choices.why: The state to avoid is a codebase full of comments telling a checker to be quiet where nobody remembers which are load-bearing.

choices.text: No flag turned on outside a pull request of its own
choices.why: One flag per pull request is good practice for the last step and is not the rule that holds the process together.

choices.text: No merge while any module is still in the override list
choices.why: The list shrinks over months; blocking merges on it would stop the work.

choices.text: No suppression at all, since each one is a defect left in place
choices.why: Some are legitimate — a stub that lies — and the requirement is the reason beside them.

prompt: Which of these is a checker's job and not a test's?
hint: One of them is about every caller in the program.

choices.text: Finding that a report totals the wrong column of the table
choices.why: Both columns are integers, so the types agree and the answer is wrong.

choices.text: Finding the caller in another file that passes the wrong type
choices.why: A checker follows every call, including the branch nobody takes and the file you were not looking at.

choices.text: Finding that a discount is applied twice on one code path
choices.why: That is behaviour, and a test is what asserts it.

choices.text: Finding that a retry loop gives up one attempt too early
choices.why: A count that is off by one is correct in every type.

prompt: A team turns the checker on and the first run says `Success: no issues found in 240 source files`. What is the reasonable reading?
hint: What does an unannotated function mean to the default settings?

choices.text: Little was checked, because unannotated functions are ones it has no opinion about
choices.why: A clean first run on a codebase with no annotations is a measurement of how much was skipped.

choices.text: The codebase is in better shape than the team expected
choices.why: It says the checker found no disagreement between annotations that mostly are not there.

choices.text: The configuration is broken, since a real codebase has errors
choices.why: The configuration is doing exactly what its defaults say.

choices.text: The cache is stale and the run reused an earlier verdict
choices.why: A stale cache is invalidated by the file contents, and this result is what the defaults produce.

prompt: The flag that makes `mypy` look inside functions that have no annotations: `--______`
hint: Three words joined by hyphens.

prompt: Where do you put a suppression so that both `mypy` and `pyright` honour it?
hint: One syntax is understood by both.

choices.text: `# type: ignore[code]`
choices.why: `pyright` accepts it too. The `# pyright: ignore` form is for a rule only `pyright` has.

choices.text: `# pyright: ignore[rule]`, which names the rule precisely
choices.why: It is precise and `mypy` treats it as an ordinary comment, so the error is still reported.

choices.text: `# noqa: code`, which the linters and the checkers share
choices.why: `# noqa` belongs to the linters and neither checker reads it.

choices.text: `# mypy: ignore[code]`, the counterpart of the `pyright` form
choices.why: That is not the syntax; `mypy` reads `# type: ignore`.

prompt: A run reports `Item "None" of "Row | None" has no attribute "city"` on a line that has never failed. What is the honest conclusion?
hint: Think about which branch the data has taken so far.

choices.text: The branch that produces `None` has not been reached yet, and the line raises when it is
choices.why: The lookup answers `None` for a row that fails validation, and the test data never does.

choices.text: The annotation on the lookup is too wide and should be narrowed to `Row`
choices.why: Narrowing the annotation to fit the data you have seen is how the report stops mentioning a real case.

choices.text: The checker cannot see the guard above the line and is reporting a false positive
choices.why: A guard above it would narrow the type and remove the error, so its absence is the finding.

choices.text: The line is unreachable, which is why it has never failed
choices.why: Unreachable code is reported differently and this line is reached with a non-`None` row.

prompt: Which of these turns a `Success` into an honest verdict without asking anybody to write an annotation?
hint: It widens what is looked at, not what is required.

choices.text: `warn_unused_ignores`, which finds the suppressions that expired
choices.why: A useful flag that says nothing about unchecked bodies.

choices.text: `disallow_untyped_defs`, which reports each function that lacks one
choices.why: It reports what has to be written, which is the paperwork rather than the defects.

choices.text: `check_untyped_defs`
choices.why: It checks inside bodies that already exist, so the errors it finds are defects rather than paperwork.

choices.text: `strict`, which is the shorthand for the whole list
choices.why: It includes the flag that demands annotations, along with a dozen others.

prompt: `mypy app/rates.py` is clean; `mypy -p app` is not. What does that tell you about where to point it?
hint: The disagreement is between two files.

choices.text: At the package, because an error lives between a definition and its caller
choices.why: The file you changed is internally consistent; the file that calls it is where the disagreement shows.

choices.text: At the file, since a package run reports errors from dependencies too
choices.why: Errors are reported in what you asked about; imports are read rather than reported.

choices.text: At either, since the same errors are found in both and only the count differs
choices.why: The single-file run reported no error at all.

choices.text: At the file first and the package in CI, so local runs stay fast
choices.why: The cache is what keeps runs fast, and a local run that misses the error has not helped you.

prompt: `json.load` gives back this type, which is how a declared return is lost without anybody noticing: `______`
hint: Three letters, capital A.

prompt: An override in `pyproject.toml` sets `disallow_untyped_defs = false` for `app.legacy.*`. A new module `app/billing/rates.py` has an unannotated function. What happens?
hint: Which modules does the override name?

choices.text: It is reported, since that exception names a different package
choices.why: That is the arrangement working: the exception list is explicit and new code falls outside it.

choices.text: It is accepted, since the top-level default applies to modules added later
choices.why: The top-level setting is the strict one; the override is what loosens it.

choices.text: It is accepted until the module is added to `files`
choices.why: It is under `app`, which `files` already names.

choices.text: It is reported as a warning rather than an error while the module is new
choices.why: There is no grace period for a new module.

prompt: Why does a checker say nothing about `total = sum(prices) * len(prices)` when an average was intended?
hint: Consider what each of the two operators produces.

choices.text: Arithmetic between numbers is outside what a checker examines
choices.why: It examines arithmetic closely — `float * None` is reported.

choices.text: `sum` returns `Any`, so nothing downstream of it is checked
choices.why: `sum` over a `list[float]` returns a float, not `Any`.

choices.text: A float times an integer is a float, which is what the annotation promised
choices.why: The types line up and the formula is wrong, and a type is not where that distinction lives.

choices.text: `len` returns an untyped value, which absorbs the multiplication
choices.why: `len` is annotated as returning an integer.

prompt: Which of these belongs in `.gitignore`?
hint: One of them is written by a run, not by a person.

choices.text: `pyrightconfig.json`, since it duplicates the `pyproject.toml`
choices.why: It is configuration somebody wrote and it belongs in the repository.

choices.text: `py.typed`, since it is an empty file with no content to track
choices.why: Its presence is the content: it is the marker saying the annotations are meant to be read.

choices.text: `.mypy_cache/`
choices.why: It holds what was worked out about each module and is what makes the second run a fraction of the first.

choices.text: `[[tool.mypy.overrides]]`, since the list changes on every merge
choices.why: It is a block inside a tracked file, and its shrinking is the record of the work.

prompt: A checker and a test are described as halves of the same job. What does the checker half cover?
hint: One of them scales over the whole program.

choices.text: Whether the pieces fit together, everywhere, including where nobody looked
choices.why: It says nothing about whether the thing they build is the thing you wanted, which is the other half.

choices.text: Whether the program produces the right answer for a chosen input
choices.why: That is what a test asserts.

choices.text: Whether the code paths a test exercised behave as the report describes
choices.why: A checker reads no test and no report of one.

choices.text: Whether the annotations somebody wrote match the data in production
choices.why: It reads no data; it compares annotations with the code around them.
